items.text: British pop star Ed Sheeran faces a major crisis on his US tour after his supporting acts all withdrew following a high-profile controversy. The conflict began when rapper Macklemore made pro-Palestinian statements and displayed images of war during a performance at Gillette Stadium in New Jersey. In response, the stadium owner and other venue managers presented Sheeran with an ultimatum : remove Macklemore or cancel the concerts. Sheeran accepted Macklemore’s removal to protect his tour crew’s livelihoods, but this decision sparked outrage among fellow artists, who all quit in protest against censorship by venue owners. At his opening solo concert in Philadelphia, Sheeran addressed the controversy directly on stage without any supporting acts. He apologized for his handling of the situation and voiced deep concern over stadium owners dictating artistic content. He condemned the October 7 attacks as horrific and described the ongoing devastation in Gaza as catastrophic. Sheeran will complete the remaining stadium dates alone. Difficult words: supporting act (a less famous performer or group that plays before the main star at a concert), venue (a place where an organized event takes place), ultimatum (a final demand or warning that threatens serious action if it is not accepted). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

Musician Ed Sheeran is facing serious problems on his American tour after all of his opening artists quit. The trouble started when rapper Macklemore showed pictures of war and called for a free Palestine during a concert. The billionaire owner of the stadium told Sheeran to remove Macklemore or cancel his shows. Sheeran let Macklemore leave because he wanted to save jobs for his crew members, but other musicians were angry about this decision. They left the tour because they believe artists should speak freely. At his first solo concert in Philadelphia, Sheeran spoke directly to the crowd. He apologized for his mistakes and called the situation in Gaza catastrophic and wrong. Sheeran will now play all the remaining big concerts completely alone with just his guitar. Difficult words: remove (to take someone or something away from a position, place, or job), solo (done by one person alone without help from others), catastrophic (when something causes great damage or suffering). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

Singer Ed Sheeran has a big problem on his tour in the US. His guest singer , Macklemore, speaks about Palestine on stage . The stadium owner gets angry. He asks Sheeran to drop Macklemore from the show. Sheeran does it. He wants to keep his tour going. After this, all the other guest singers quit the tour. They think that artists must speak freely on stage. At his next big show in Philadelphia, Sheeran plays alone, only with his guitar. Sheeran says sorry to his fans for making mistakes . He calls the war in Gaza terrible. He will finish all his concerts alone. Difficult words: guest singer (a singer who sings before the main singer), stage (a floor up high where an actor or singer performs in front of people), mistake (a wrong action). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

Jared Kushner, Donald Trump’s son-in-law, serves as a high-level diplomatic envoy despite having no prior background in public service. Kushner grew up in a prominent New Jersey real estate family and became a trusted adviser during Trump’s initial political campaign. Although foreign business ties raised security concerns and blocked his clearance , those issues were ultimately dismissed, and he was granted access to international negotiations in regions like Gaza and Ukraine. Kushner’s dual role as a private businessman and diplomat has raised serious conflict-of-interest questions. After leaving government, his private equity firm secured massive investments from Saudi Arabia’s sovereign wealth fund. While diplomats recognize his ability to communicate directly with the president, experts caution that negotiating through Kushner remains unpredictable given Trump’s changing decisions. Despite potential security and financial concerns, Kushner’s position within the president’s family ensures his continued global influence. Difficult words: envoy (a messenger or official representative sent by a government to deal with another country), prior (happening or existing before a particular time or event), clearance (official permission given to someone to see secret or confidential government information), dual (having two parts, roles, or aspects at the same time). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

Jared Kushner, the son-in-law of Donald Trump, is one of the most powerful diplomats in the United States. He grew up in a wealthy real estate family and later joined Trump’s team as a close adviser. Although security officials worried about his foreign business connections, he was given special access to high-level diplomatic talks in places like Ukraine and the Middle East. Many critics worry about conflicts of interest because Kushner created a business that received billions of dollars from Saudi Arabia. But foreign leaders often work with him because they know he speaks directly to the president. Experts say having a family member act as a private businessman and international diplomat creates a new and unusual situation in modern American history. Difficult words: diplomat (an official who represents their country in talks and relations with other nations), real estate (land and buildings), conflict of interest (a situation where a person’s private life or business gains could unfairly influence their official duty or job decisions). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

Jared Kushner is Donald Trump’s son-in-law . He works as a very important diplomat for the United States. But he also has his own business. Some people worry about his foreign money and business. But he still has an important job in the government. Kushner talks to leaders in other countries to help stop wars in places like Ukraine. Many leaders like to talk to him because he is part of the president’s family. But some people say that mixing family, money, and government work can cause problems. Kushner stays very close to the president, so his power is very strong today. Difficult words: son-in-law (the husband of a person’s daughter), diplomat (an official who represents their country in other countries), foreign (connected to another country). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

International test results reveal a sharp decline in teenage reading skills across 91 countries since 2012. Experts argue that digital screens are transforming young readers into hasty readers or skimmers . Because students read quickly on digital devices without allocating time and effort to complex comprehension, they fail to develop critical thinking skills. Furthermore, rising reliance on AI text generators like ChatGPT lets students skip essential writing processes, which further weakens the neural circuits required for deep reading and critical analysis. This decline poses significant risks to democratic societies. Without strong reading skills, future voters become far more vulnerable to misinformation, demagoguery , and algorithmic control. However, experts emphasize that this trend can be changed. Countries like Estonia and Singapore successfully integrate technology in schools to support cognitive skills rather than passive consumption. Reversing the decline requires starting early by reading to children and establishing daily habits of reading challenging printed books. Difficult words: hasty (hurried), skimmer (a person who reads through a text quickly to get the main idea without reading every word carefully), neural circuit (a population of interconnected neurons in the brain that work together to process information and carry out functions), demagoguery (political activity or speech that seeks support by appealing to the desires and prejudices of ordinary people rather than by using rational argument). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

Tests show that teenage reading skills are dropping rapidly around the world. Experts say reading on digital screens turns young people into hasty readers. Instead of reading carefully, students skim texts. This means they don’t fully understand what they read. Using AI tools to write assignments also stops students from practicing deep reading and writing. This trend is dangerous for society and democracy. If young people cannot understand complex information, they cannot make good decisions as informed voters. But we can fix this problem. Countries like Estonia use technology to make students think harder, not to make work too easy. Parents can help by reading to young children and encouraging everyone to read physical books for 20 minutes every day. Difficult words: hasty (hurried), assignment (a piece of work or task), encourage (to give support or hope to someone to do something). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

Reading test scores for teenagers are falling in many countries. Experts say that screens make young people read too fast. Children skim words on their phones and tablets. They do not understand the main ideas. Also, using AI to write paper assignments stops the brain from learning. This is bad for the future. People need to read to think well. If not, they easily believe fake news and bad information. But we can change this situation. Parents should read books to young children every day. Reading real books for 20 minutes a day helps the brain grow strong and keeps reading skills safe. Difficult words: score (the number of points in a test or game), skim (to read something quickly), assignment (a piece of work or task). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

The long-standing conflict in Yemen is intensifying as Houthi forces launch a major offensive against Saudi-backed government troops in the eastern province of Al Jawf. Media released by the Houthi group shows extensive battlefield footage, including destroyed armored vehicles, heavy machine-gun fire from pickup trucks, and intense ground fighting across desert trenches. Houthi forces claim to have inflicted heavy losses on government troops as their offensive gains momentum . In response, the Saudi-backed coalition has released aerial footage depicting retaliatory airstrikes aimed at stopping the Houthi advance and destroying military equipment. As the violence spreads, innocent civilians bear the burden of the expanding war. Families are fleeing active battle zones on foot under heavy gunfire, and they often travel for days without food or water. Many displaced residents now arrive at makeshift camps outside Aden while the broader conflict continues to escalate. Difficult words: inflict (to cause something unpleasant or painful to happen to someone else), momentum (the force or speed that keeps an activity moving forward and growing faster), retaliatory (done to pay someone back for a harmful action they did to you first), makeshift (made quickly using whatever is available to serve a purpose for a short time). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

Fighting in Yemen is getting worse as Houthi forces attack Saudi-backed government troops in the Al Jawf area. Houthi media showed videos of destroyed military trucks, rockets, and heavy fighting in the desert. The Houthis say they killed many enemy soldiers and destroyed their weapons during several days of conflict. At the same time, the Saudi-backed government released air force pictures showing strikes against Houthi fighters and equipment to stop their advance . Because of the heavy fighting and air attacks, many families escaped their homes. People walked at night without food or water while bullets flew around them. Many displaced families now live in simple tents in camps near Aden, and hope the dangerous conflict will stop soon. Difficult words: enemy (a person, group, or country that fights against you), advance (moving forward toward a destination or goal), displaced (when someone must leave home because of war or a dangerous situation). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

The war in Yemen is getting very bad. Houthi fighters are attacking government soldiers in the desert. Videos show burning trucks, big guns, and explosions . Houthi forces say that they are winning the fight. The Saudi- backed government is using planes to attack Houthi soldiers from the sky. Because of the dangerous fighting, many families must run away from their homes. People walk at night with no food, no water, and no money. Now, many mothers, fathers, and children live in small tents in camps. They need help because the war is starting in new places. Difficult words: explosion (when a bomb goes off with a loud noise), backed (when a person or group helps someone else with money or things), tent (a shelter made of cloth which people often use for camping). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

European Central Bank President Christine Lagarde has unveiled ten shortlisted design concepts for future euro banknotes, selected from over 1,200 proposals. The designs represent two main themes chosen to reflect European identity. The first theme focuses on prominent cultural figures in history, including artist Leonardo da Vinci, opera singer Maria Callas, scientist Marie Curie, and composer Ludwig van Beethoven. The second theme highlights nature and depicts various European bird species in river landscapes alongside major European Union institutions to emphasize Europe’s biodiversity and environmental protection. For the first time, European citizens will participate in selecting the final theme through an online survey hosted on the central bank’s website. Following the public vote and final design selection, technical preparation and production stages will begin. The new banknotes, which will be worth from 5 to 500 euros, are expected to enter circulation starting from the end of 2026. Difficult words: shortlisted (put on a small, final list of the best people or ideas chosen from a larger group), biodiversity (the variety of different types of plants, animals, and living things in a natural area), circulation (the movement of money as it is passed from person to person when buying and selling things). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

The European Central Bank has shown ten finalist designs for new euro cash notes . Over 1,200 ideas were sent in, but leaders chose two big ideas to show European culture and nature. The first idea features famous historic leaders in art, science, and music, such as Leonardo da Vinci, Maria Callas, Marie Curie, and Beethoven. The second idea features wild birds and beautiful rivers, and shows the need to protect nature and animals across Europe. People living in the EU can vote for their favorite idea in an online survey on the bank’s website. After the vote, the central bank will start printing the new paper money. People are expected to start using these new euro notes from the end of 2026. Difficult words: finalist (a person, team, or idea that reaches the last stage of a competition), note (a piece of paper money), feature (to show, include, or give special attention to something or someone as an important part). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

The European Central Bank shows ten designs for new euro money. Bank leaders choose from 1,200 ideas. They pick two main topics . The first topic shows famous people like Leonardo da Vinci, Marie Curie, and Beethoven. The second topic shows birds and rivers to help protect nature. Now, people who live in Europe can choose their favorite design. They can vote on the bank’s website. After the vote, the bank will make the new paper money. People will start to use the new euro money at the end of 2026. Difficult words: topic (the main idea), favorite (when many people like a person or thing), vote (to officially choose a person, idea, or plan). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

Hello students, Do you want to learn English effectively? We have a special book for you. The book is written in three levels. You can learn English for your level when you read this book. Level 1 is written in the present tense. Level 2 is written in the past tense. Level 3 is written in grammar which is important for intermediate students. The name of the book is Robinson Crusoe. You can find the book at www.robinsoncrusoeinlevels.com . You can read one chapter every day. You can learn new words and grammar suitable for your level. With this book, you can learn English naturally by using the language. There are 1780 individual words in the book. We hope you will enjoy the book. News in Levels team

Australian athlete Joanna Wietrzyk won her age category at a Hyrox indoor fitness competition in Beijing, but her victory created significant controversy. While competing, she suffered severe bowel incontinence and left feces on shared equipment such as rowers and carpeted areas. Wietrzyk finished the race in just over an hour and later shared a photo from a hospital bed on an IV drip with the caption A win is a win . Opinions on the incident are deeply divided. Some fans praised her determination, mental strength, and refusal to give up under extreme physical distress. However, critics, commentators, and fellow participants highlighted the serious biological hazard her condition presented to other competitors. Many questioned why organizers didn’t intervene and stop her to provide medical help, especially since existing rules already penalized spitting and littering. Organizers had to close affected lanes, replace carpet, and deep clean the venue overnight, while debate continues over athlete health and safety protocols. Difficult words: incontinence (losing control of your body so you cannot hold in urine or poop), IV drip (a small bag of liquid medicine or water connected to a needle in a person’s arm), biological hazard (something from a living body, like germs, blood, or waste, that can cause sickness to other people). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

Australian fitness athlete Joanna Wietrzyk won a big indoor competition in Beijing, China. But her victory caused a lot of discussion because she was very sick during the race. Wietrzyk had severe stomach problems and left feces on shared sports equipment and carpets. After winning, she went to the hospital and posted a picture on social media. In the post, she wrote A win is a win . Some people praised her because she worked very hard and didn’t stop although she had problems. But many other people were angry. They said her condition was unsafe and dirty for other athletes. People also asked why the organizers didn’t stop her to give her medical care. The event organizers had to close some lanes, change the carpet, and clean everything carefully. The story shows a big debate about sports rules and athlete health. Difficult words: feces (solid waste that comes out of the body after digesting food), condition (how healthy or fit you are), debate (a discussion about a topic). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

Joanna Wietrzyk is an athlete from Australia. She wins a big fitness race in Beijing, China. But she was very sick during the event. Joanna has bad stomach problems. She has feces on her legs. She makes the sports equipment dirty . After the race, she goes to a hospital. She puts a photo on the internet. She is happy to win the race. Some people say that she is very strong. Other people say that it is dirty and dangerous for other runners. Nobody stops Joanna during the race. People on the internet ask why. The workers at the event must clean the room. They put down new carpets. Many people now talk about how safe sport is for athletes. Difficult words: feces (poop), equipment (the tools or machines which you need to do an activity or sport), dirty (not clean). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

Tech executives are divided on AI regulation. OpenAI boss Sam Altman acknowledged public fears while urging trust in developers. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang opposed new laws and stated that companies should self-regulate product safety. Sanders warned that AI risks could exceed those of nuclear weapons, and urged lawmakers to prevent corporations from socializing the risks while keeping the financial profits. Politicians across the political spectrum are demanding strict restrictions; however, US President Donald Trump has dismissed safety fears surrounding AI as a hoax . He argued against slowing down development because the country that leads in AI wins globally. Trump highlighted the technology’s immense economic potential and compared its value to big industries like oil and diamonds. Experts emphasize that the United States must establish strong domestic oversight to set international standards. Tech companies often leverage the idea of a global race with China to justify moving forward without adequate laws. Difficult words: socialize (to share the cost, debt, or risk of something across the whole community instead of one private company paying for it), hoax (a plan to trick people into believing something that is not true), immense (extremely large or great in size, amount, or degree), leverage (to use something, like power or an advantage, to achieve a specific result). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

US President Donald Trump called AI safety fears a hoax and said the country must win the global AI race. He believes AI will bring economic growth bigger than oil or diamonds. But many people and experts disagree on how to manage this new technology. OpenAI leader Sam Altman says people should trust tech companies, while Nvidia’s CEO believes businesses should control their own safety rules without new government laws. Some politicians warned that AI could be more dangerous than nuclear weapons. Many critics worry that big companies want all the profits , but at the same time, ordinary people will be at risk. Experts argue that the US needs strict rules to protect people and set a good example for the rest of the world. Difficult words: hoax (a plan to trick people), economic growth (when a country produces more things and services than in the past), profit (the money you have left after you pay all costs). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

US President Donald Trump says that fears about AI are not real. He wants the US to win the AI race. It will make the country strong. Some tech leaders say that people should trust them to make AI safe. They do not want new laws. But many politicians want strong safety rules. Some politicians say that AI can be very dangerous, even more than nuclear bombs. Some people believe that big companies only want to make money. Normal people will take all the risks . Experts say that we need good rules today to keep everyone safe in the future. Difficult words: fear (when you are scared of something), trust (to believe that something is good or safe), risk (a chance that something bad or dangerous may happen). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

Astronomers have identified the most luminous object ever observed in the far reaches of space, named J0529-4351. Detected by the Very Large Telescope in Chile, this object is a quasar , shining 500 trillion times brighter than the Sun. It hosts the fastest-growing black hole ever recorded, consuming mass equal to one Sun daily. Initially mistaken for a nearby star, J0529-4351’s true distance of 12 billion light-years emphasizes its intrinsic brightness. Quasars like this one, with supermassive black holes at their cores, challenge existing theories about the early universe’s formation. The discovery underscores the mystery of how such massive black holes formed so early in cosmic history. Scientists speculate that these findings may provide insights into the fundamental nature of black hole formation shortly after the Big Bang. Difficult words: luminous (emitting a lot of light), quasar (a highly energetic distant celestial object), intrinsic (natural, essential). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

Scientists discovered the brightest object in the universe, and they named it J0529-4351. They used the Very Large Telescope in Chile. The object is a quasar, a very big object which emits large amounts of energy. It shines 500 trillion times brighter than the Sun and hosts the fastest-growing black hole scientists ever recorded. The distance from Earth is 12 billion light-years, and it emphasizes the object’s brightness. These findings challenge all we know about the early universe and how it formed. It suggests that black holes formed shortly after the Big Bang. Understanding this could help scientists find out what happened in the early days of the universe. Difficult words: emit (produce gas or energy), emphasize (to make something seem important), challenge (to bring questions if something is valid). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

Scientists find the brightest object in the universe. It is as bright as 500 trillion suns. Scientists use a big telescope in Chile to find the object. They call it J0529-4351. There is a black hole inside. It is the fastest-growing black hole ever. At first, scientists think that it is a nearby star. The object is 12 billion light-years away from us. This makes it even more amazing. It is a special kind of object called a quasar. Quasars are very bright and they produce a lot of energy. This discovery makes scientists wonder how big black holes form so early in the universe. There are many questions now. Difficult words: telescope (a tool which we use to see things far away), discovery (a new thing which we find), question (when we ask something to get information). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

A major generational shift is transforming childhood into an era of intense consumerism . Today, more toys are sold to adults than to children, while kids, often referred to as Generation Alpha, are opting for iPhones, adult skincare, and expensive colognes instead. Driven by viral TikTok trends like looksmaxxing and beauty tutorials, eight-year-olds are doing complex multi-step grooming routines. This shift has led to instances where young children apply harsh acids and retinols meant for older skin, which is causing physical damage. Corporations and beauty brands aggressively capitalize on this trend. They view young children as lifelong customers and adjust marketing strategies specifically toward them. Meanwhile, over 60 percent of surveyed students express a desire to become influencers, and they frequently neglect formal education and creative play. While social media platforms and corporate marketing build this consumer pipeline, millennial parents finance these purchases. Critics argue that parents must intervene to restore traditional, screen-free childhood experiences. Difficult words: consumerism (buying and wanting a lot of new things, often more than you really need), cologne (a type of nice-smelling liquid that people put on their skin or clothes), looksmaxxing (a popular internet word for trying to make your physical appearance look as good as possible), capitalize (to take advantage of a situation to make money or get a benefit). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

Today, adults buy more toys than children do, while young kids want adult items like smartphones, makeup, and expensive perfume. Thanks to social media apps like TikTok, young boys and girls are watching videos about beauty and grooming routines . Many eight-year-old children are using adult skincare products, which can hurt their skin. Big companies are happy about this trend because they make a lot of money selling products to young buyers. In addition, many children now say they want to be famous online influencers instead of going to school or playing outside. Although big tech companies and advertisers encourage this consumer behavior , parents are the ones buying these products. Experts say parents should limit screen time and help their children enjoy a real, simple childhood. Difficult words: grooming routine (the regular steps you do every day to keep your body clean and neat), encourage (to give someone confidence or hope, or to persuade them to do something), behavior (the way a person acts or does things). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

Today, many children do not play with normal toys. Instead, they want iPhones, adult makeup, and body sprays. Small children watch social media videos on phones and iPads. They see adults who use beauty products. Children want to do the same. But using adult skincare can hurt a child’s skin. Big stores and companies make a lot of money from young buyers. Many young kids do not want to go to school. They want to become famous online. Parents spend a lot of money on these things for their children. Experts say that kids need less screen time, fewer products, and more time to play outside like in the past . Difficult words: adult (a person who is not a child anymore), famous (when many people know someone or something), past (the time before now). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

The UK government will allow mayors in England to introduce a tourist tax on overnight stays before 2029. The levy will apply to all accommodation types, including hotels, B&Bs, and short-term rentals, regardless of the visitor’s nationality or purpose. While the charge is uncapped, local leaders, including London’s mayor, expect to keep it under 5% of the total accommodation cost. Similar fees are already operational in Manchester and Edinburgh, following widespread adoption across continental Europe. However, the hospitality sector has strongly criticized the decision. Experts warn that a 5% tax could reduce tourism spending by 1.8 billion pounds (2.1 billion euros) and destroy nearly 33,000 jobs by 2030. Furthermore, extra fees might deter both international and domestic travelers and drive them toward destinations without visitor levies. Difficult words: levy (an official amount of money, such as a tax, that a government or organization collects), operational (ready to use, working, or actively in service), hospitality sector (businesses that provide services like hotels, restaurants, bars, and travel). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

England will soon allow local mayors to charge a tourist tax on overnight hotel stays. The tax will cover all types of places to stay, like hotels, B&Bs, and holiday homes. Mayors can choose the exact price, but most plan to keep it under 5% of the total room bill. Cities like Manchester, which charges 1 pound (1.14 euros) per room, and Edinburgh already use similar fees. The new tax will likely start before 2029. Many businesses in the tourism industry are unhappy about the new tax. They worry that visitors will choose other places to travel to avoid paying extra fees, which could lead to a 1.8 billion pound (2.1 billion euros) loss in tourism spending. Studies show that many tourists might stay fewer nights or spend less money. Mayors don’t have to introduce the tax, and some local leaders already said no to the plan. Difficult words: mayor (an elected leader of a city or town government), likely (expected to happen or very probable), avoid (to stay away from a person, place, or situation). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

England will let local leaders add a small tax to overnight hotel stays. People who stay in hotels, B&Bs, or holiday homes will pay a little extra money, usually under 5% of the room cost. Some cities like Manchester already have a tax of 1 pound (1.14 euros) per room. The new plan will start before 2029. Many hotel owners do not like this new tax. They worry that visitors will go to other places to save money. Studies show that a 10-pound (11.40 euros) fee might make people visit less. But each local leader can choose to use the tax or say no to it. Difficult words: add (to put something together with something else), tax (money that people must pay to the government to pay for public services), fee (money which you pay for a particular service). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

Czech visionary Josef Průša has redefined additive manufacturing through his pioneering 3D printing technology. Originally a student fascinated by music equipment, he engineered his own self-replicating 3D printer, an innovation that soon became an industry standard. In 2012, he left university to establish Prusa Research, which has since evolved into a global enterprise based in Prague. The firm employs more than 1,200 people, exports worldwide, and generates annual revenues exceeding 160 million euros. Its award-winning machines are used by leading institutions such as NASA, CERN, and MIT, as well as numerous startups. Průša’s philosophy centers on decentralizing production and stimulating European innovation. By making high-quality 3D printing accessible, he envisions a future where creativity, technology, and sustainability merge to reshape manufacturing across the continent. Difficult words: visionary (a person with original ideas about what the future could be like), decentralize (to spread control or production away from one main place to several smaller ones), merge (to join two or more things together to become one). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

Josef Průša is a Czech entrepreneur and engineer who became one of Europe’s most influential people in 3D printing. As a student, he experimented with music technology and built his first 3D printer to make customized parts. His design quickly gained global interest, and in 2012, he founded Prusa Research in Prague. The company now employs over 1,000 people and sells 3D printers to customers on every continent, including large organizations such as NASA, Mercedes, and MIT. Průša’s open-source approach inspires countless small companies to innovate using cheaper printers locally. He believes 3D printing can bring manufacturing back to Europe by helping entrepreneurs design, produce, and compete independently. Difficult words: entrepreneur (someone who starts and manages their own business), influential (having the power to change people’s opinions or the way things develop), customized (made or changed to fit one person’s or company’s special needs), open-source approach (a way of working where people share their software or designs freely so others can use, change, and improve them). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

Josef Průša is a Czech inventor . He changes the world of 3D printing. As a student, he likes working with music equipment. He needs special parts for his projects. So, he decides to build his own 3D printer. His design becomes very popular. In 2012, he starts a company called Prusa Research in Prague. Today, the company sells printers all over the world and works with big organizations like NASA and Mercedes. Many small businesses also use his printers to make creative products. Josef Průša believes that 3D printing can help more people create and build new things in Europe and beyond . Difficult words: inventor (a person who creates something new), creative (able to make or think of new interesting ideas), beyond (further than). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

Gambian President Adama Barrow promised to improve the country’s severe power outages by the end of October. His announcement followed intense overnight protests in the capital, Banjul, and surrounding areas. Demonstrators blocked roads, set fires, and marched toward the headquarters of the national energy provider, NAWEC. Police used tear gas to disperse the crowds. Residents expressed frustration over spoiled food and interrupted businesses after enduring blackouts lasting up to 48 hours during extreme summer heat. President Barrow declared the crisis a national security issue and an emergency. To address the shortage, the government is installing a new 24-megawatt generator and planning a 50-megawatt solar power plant. NAWEC officials attributed the blackouts to rising demand, climate change, and Middle Eastern conflict impacting imports. These unrests mark a major escalation just months before the December presidential election, where Barrow is seeking a third term. A flashbulb memory is a vivid recollection of learning about a major, highly emotional public event, such as the September 11 terror attacks. Although people feel absolute confidence in these memories, research shows they are not entirely accurate. Memories are dynamic ; each time a person retrieves one, the hippocampus updates it with new information from media or conversations. In fact, studies reveal that people alter roughly 40 percent of their personal details within a year. Unlike regular memories, emotional events activate the amygdala, which focuses attention and embeds the experience more strongly. These memories also strengthen social connection, because they create a shared sense of identity among groups. Even prominent figures, including President George W. Bush, have famously mixed up the timeline of how they learned about the 9/11 attacks due to repeated exposure to news footage. Because modern media is highly fragmented, widespread flashbulb memories shared by whole nations may become less common in the future. Difficult words: vivid (producing very clear, detailed, and bright pictures in your mind), dynamic (constantly changing, active, or developing rather than staying the same), retrieve (to find and bring back information from memory or storage), embed (to fix something firmly and deeply into something else). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

A flashbulb memory is a strong memory of where you were during a big world event, like the September 11 attacks. People feel very sure about these memories, but scientists say they can be wrong. Every time we remember something, our brain changes the details. Studies show that people change about 40 percent of the details after one year. Big emotions change how the brain saves memories. Strong feelings make us remember events clearly, but we still make mistakes. For example, President George W. Bush misremembered how he first heard about the 9/11 plane crash. Flashbulb memories help us feel connected to other people because we shared the same big experience . Today, because news comes from many different sources, fewer large groups will share the exact same flashbulb memories in the future. Difficult words: flashbulb memory (a sudden, extremely clear, and detailed memory of a shocking event), misremember (to remember something incorrectly), experience (something that happens to you). In a rundown neighborhood on the outskirts of Havana, Cuban agronomist Lorenzo Suarez has transformed his home into an urban oasis that contains 100 different orchid species and hybrids . While Cuba faces severe economic difficulties, including frequent blackouts and resource shortages, Suarez uses his specialized skills as an agricultural engineer to breed new flowers. Unlike growers in other countries who raise plants for commercial profit, Suarez is motivated by a passion for creating unique plant varieties. In 2009, he created Cuba’s first ornamental hybrid, named Bella Lorena . Today, his main focus is combining native Cuban orchids with imported varieties. Through this careful breeding process, he aims to produce eye-catching hybrids that can easily adapt to rising local temperatures. By making these cultivated varieties available, Suarez hopes to discourage people from harvesting rare and endangered wild orchids directly from Cuba’s forests, where approximately 300 native species are currently threatened by human activity and environmental change. Difficult words: rundown (in very bad condition because of age or lack of care), agronomist (an expert in the science of farming and growing plants), hybrid (a plant or animal bred from two different species or types), cultivated (grown and cared for by humans, not wild). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

The far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party achieved a historic victory in the Saxony-Anhalt state election. It won 43.8% of the vote and secured 39 of the 83 parliamentary seats. The ruling conservative Christian Democrats (CDU) suffered a major defeat when it dropped to just 17%. Although the AfD fell three seats short of an absolute majority, its massive win has caused significant political turbulence across Germany. Experts point to voter dissatisfaction with the federal government, concerns over migration, and the popularity of local candidates as drivers of the AfD’s success. The election places immense pressure on the CDU’s policy that strictly prohibits cooperation with the far right. With traditional coalition building extremely complicated, the AfD is actively attempting to persuade individual lawmakers to defect . If the AfD influences the state government, it plans radical policy changes regarding education, culture, and migration enforcement. Difficult words: turbulence (a state of confusion, violence, or unstable movement), immense (extremely large or great), defect (to leave one group, country, or political party to join an opposing one). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

A mysterious floating island covered with growing trees has recently appeared in Williston Lake, Canada, which surprised both residents and experts. A resident captured video footage of the unusual island in July, but it vanished just a few days later, a movement confirmed by satellite imagery. The mystery deepened on August 31, when the island was photographed again in the reservoir. Experts believe the phenomenon was created over many years. Trees had been growing undisturbed on piles of woody debris along the shoreline. Recently, rising water levels in the reservoir lifted the heavy mass of wood and soil and set it free to float across the water. Representatives of the government utility managing the dam suggest that during the periods when the island seemed to disappear, it had simply drifted back toward the shore or moved out of view before floating away again. Difficult words: vanish (to disappear completely and suddenly), phenomenon (something strange or unusual that can be seen), utility (a company that provides a public service, such as electricity, water, or gas). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

The experts explained that when the water level in the lake went up, it lifted the ground and set the small island free to float on the water. When people couldn’t see it, the island probably just floated to a different shore . This makes sense, but for many people, it is still something mysterious . Difficult words: disappear (to go away from a place so that you cannot be seen), shore (the land along the edge of a lake, sea, or river), mysterious (strange or difficult to understand or explain). A specialty butter shop in Paris, France, is highlighting the incredible flavor complexity and diversity of a beloved French staple . The shop offers around 30 different flavored varieties that range from savory choices like wild garlic, herbs, onion, and seaweed to sweet options like chocolate, vanilla, and raspberry. Different regions produce butter with varying fat percentages, which creates unique tastes and textures. Once people sample artisanal , high-quality butter, they quickly discover a completely new culinary experience that standard supermarket butter cannot match. Quality butter melts smoothly on the tongue and offers a rich creaminess and deep, nuanced flavors. This fascinating variety of ingredients and regional production methods explains why interest in premium butter is growing among food lovers around the world. Difficult words: complexity (having many different parts, flavors, or details that make something interesting or difficult to understand), staple (a main or important food that people eat regularly), savory (having a salty or spicy taste, not sweet), artisanal (traditionally made by hand using high-quality ingredients). You can watch the video news lower on this page.
